headline: Fusion startups attract over $100M in funding
summary: Advances in AI, computer chips, and superconducting magnets fuel a wave of investment in fusion energy.
details: Fusion power, once a distant dream, is rapidly becoming a tangible reality thanks to significant investor interest. Startups are leveraging breakthroughs in AI, advanced computer chips, and powerful superconducting magnets to develop commercially viable fusion power plants.

A major milestone was the U.S. Department of Energy's announcement of a controlled fusion reaction producing more power than consumed by the lasers, achieving scientific breakeven. While commercial breakeven remains a goal, this proved the underlying science is sound.

Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS) leads the pack, having raised nearly $3 billion, including an $863 million round in August. They are building Sparc, a tokamak reactor designed to produce power at commercially relevant levels, with operation expected by late 2026 or early 2027.

CFS plans to construct Arc, a 400-megawatt commercial power plant, later this decade. Google has already committed to purchasing half of its output, highlighting the growing commercial interest in fusion energy.

TAE Technologies, formerly Tri Alpha Energy, uses a field-reversed configuration and plans to merge with Trump Media & Technology Group in an all-stock transaction valued at $6 billion. Before this, TAE had raised $1.79 billion.

Helion, based in Washington, has the most aggressive timeline, aiming to produce electricity from its reactor in 2028. Its first customer will be Microsoft, signaling major tech companies' commitment to the future of fusion energy.
